title: YOU SAY GOD COMES FIRST… BUT YOUR DAILY SCHEDULE MAY BE TELLING A DIFFERENT STORY
paragraphs: YOU SAY GOD COMES FIRST… BUT YOUR DAILY SCHEDULE MAY BE TELLING A DIFFERENT STORY

What if the greatest danger to your relationship with Jesus isn't that you've stopped believing in Him… but that you've become so busy living your life that you've learned how to live most of it without Him?
There is something deeply uncomfortable about opening your Bible, reading the words of Jesus, and suddenly realizing that the person being confronted by Scripture is you.
Not your unbelieving neighbor.
Not the Christian who stopped attending church.
Not that person on Facebook who posts Bible verses but lives differently behind closed doors.
You.
The person who says, “God is my number one.”
The person who believes Jesus died for their sins.
The person who genuinely wants to go to heaven, loves worship music, and knows exactly what to say when someone asks about their faith.
But there's a question that might expose something we have spent years avoiding.
If someone followed you for seven days, without hearing a single word about what you believe, would they know that Jesus Christ is the Lord of your life?
Not by your Facebook biography.
Not by the cross around your neck.
Not by the Christian quotations you share.
But by the way you actually live.
By what receives your first attention in the morning.
By what occupies your thoughts when nobody is watching.
By what you refuse to miss.
By what you always find time for.
And by what you repeatedly promise God you will do… tomorrow.
Because sometimes the most revealing testimony about our spiritual priorities isn't spoken by our mouths.
It's written in the ordinary decisions of our daily lives.
And before you become defensive, please understand something.

This isn't about condemning someone who works twelve hours to feed their family. It isn't about shaming an exhausted mother who barely has time to sit down, a student overwhelmed by responsibilities, or someone struggling with illness, grief, or depression.
God sees those burdens.
He knows the difference between someone who is genuinely overwhelmed and someone who has quietly become comfortable keeping Him at a distance.
This is about something deeper.
It's about the possibility that we have given Jesus the highest position in our religious vocabulary while leaving Him outside the ordinary decisions that shape our lives.
And the frightening part?
We can become so accustomed to that contradiction that we stop noticing it.
You wake up.
Your alarm rings.
Before your feet touch the floor, your hand reaches for your phone.
Notifications.
Messages.
News.
Facebook.
Videos.
Someone else's vacation.
Someone else's success.
Someone else's argument.
Someone else's life.
Ten minutes become thirty.
Thirty become forty-five.
Eventually, you rush to prepare for work, school, or whatever the day demands.
You remember you haven't prayed.
So you whisper something hurried.
“Lord, thank You for this day. Please protect me. Amen.”
And off you go.
There is nothing wrong with a short prayer. Some of the most sincere prayers in Scripture are remarkably brief.
But somewhere in the rush, a painful question remains.
How did we become so available to everything else and so unavailable to the One we claim matters most?
We can spend an hour watching strangers explain their lives.
But five minutes of stillness before God feels uncomfortable.
We can remember the release date of a television series.
But forget the Scripture we read yesterday.
We can rearrange an entire evening for entertainment.
But when the opportunity comes to worship, serve, pray, or encourage someone, suddenly our schedule becomes impossible.
We can stay awake long past midnight scrolling through things we will barely remember tomorrow.
Yet open the Bible and immediately feel sleepy.
And still, with complete confidence, we say:
“God comes first.”
But what does first actually mean?
Jesus addressed this issue with a clarity that leaves little room for comfortable excuses.
In Matthew 6:33, He said:
“But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” (KJV)
In the original Greek, the expression is:
ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ
Zēteite de prōton tēn basileian tou theou kai tēn dikaiosynēn autou.
“Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness.”
The word ζητεῖτε (zēteite) comes from a verb meaning to seek, pursue, or strive for. In this command, the present-tense form naturally communicates an ongoing pursuit.
And πρῶτον (prōton) means “first.”
Not merely first in a morning routine.
Not simply first on a list of religious activities.
But first in priority.
Jesus was speaking in the context of anxiety about food, clothing, and life's necessities. He wasn't teaching people to abandon their responsibilities or pretend that material needs don't matter.
He was teaching them not to let those needs displace their trust in their heavenly Father.
That's important.
Because seeking God first does not necessarily mean spending more minutes reading Scripture than working, sleeping, caring for children, or earning a living.
It means living under His rule in all those things.
It means your work belongs to Him.
Your relationships belong to Him.
Your finances belong to Him.
Your decisions belong to Him.
Your ambitions, your entertainment, your private conversations, your hidden habits, and even your plans for tomorrow are brought before His authority.
God being first is not merely about where He appears on your schedule. It's about whether He has authority over the whole schedule.
And that's where the question becomes personal.
Because a person can attend church every Sunday and still live Monday through Saturday as though Jesus has nothing to say about their choices.
A person can read the Bible every morning and still mistreat their spouse every evening.
A person can pray for financial blessing while refusing to practice honesty in business.
A person can serve in ministry and quietly neglect the people God has entrusted to their care.
A person can spend hours studying theology while refusing to forgive someone who wounded them.
Religious activity alone does not prove spiritual surrender.
And a crowded schedule alone does not prove spiritual failure.
The deeper question is whether our lives are being shaped by the Jesus we profess to follow.
There's a story in Luke 10 that becomes especially uncomfortable when you read it slowly.
Jesus entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home.
Martha was busy serving.
Her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet, listening to His teaching.
Martha became frustrated.
She was working while Mary was sitting.
Eventually, she approached Jesus and complained.
“Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.” (Luke 10:40, KJV)
You can almost hear the exhaustion in her voice.
She wasn't doing something obviously sinful.
She was showing hospitality.
She was trying to serve Jesus.
And that's what makes the moment so revealing.
Jesus answered:
“Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42, KJV)
The Greek text describes Martha as distracted by much serving.
περιεσπᾶτο περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν
Periespato peri pollēn diakonian.
The verb periespato conveys being pulled away or distracted.
Martha was not rebuked because serving was evil.
She was gently corrected because her preoccupation had pulled her attention away from the One she was serving.
And perhaps that's where some of us are living.
We're busy building the life we once prayed for.
Busy providing for the family God gave us.
Busy maintaining the responsibilities we believe He entrusted to us.
Busy working.
Busy organizing.
Busy achieving.
Busy trying to survive.
And somewhere along the way, we become so occupied with the things surrounding our relationship with God that we neglect the relationship itself.
We know how to work for Him.
But we've forgotten how to be still before Him.
We know how to ask Him for help.
But we've forgotten how to listen to His Word.
We know how to speak about Jesus.
But we're slowly losing the tenderness of walking with Jesus.
And sometimes the saddest sentence a believer can whisper is:
“Lord, I don't know when it happened… but I've become distant from You.”
Maybe that's you.
Maybe you remember when you first surrendered your life to Christ.
You weren't perfect.
You didn't understand everything.
But something was different.
You wanted to read the Bible.
You wanted to pray.
You wanted to understand the Gospel.
You were hungry for truth.
When you sinned, your heart was troubled.
When you heard about the cross, you remembered what Jesus had done for you.
You didn't just believe that God existed.
You wanted to know Him.
But then life happened.
Bills increased.
Responsibilities multiplied.
Disappointments came.
Someone hurt you.
A prayer seemed unanswered.
You became tired.
You stopped reading Scripture regularly.
Then stopped praying except when something went wrong.
Then began missing fellowship.
Then started making compromises that once would have troubled your conscience.
Not all at once.
Little by little.
Until one day, you realized that you could go through an entire day without seriously considering what Christ wanted from you.
And the most unsettling part was that your life still looked relatively normal.
You still went to work.
Still laughed.
Still posted.
Still celebrated birthdays.
Still made plans.
Still told people you were Christian.
But something inside had grown quiet.
You hadn't necessarily rejected Jesus with your words.
You had simply learned how to organize your life without regularly turning toward Him.
And if that description hurts, don't rush past it.
Not every painful realization is meant to destroy you.
Sometimes the truth exposes what grace is ready to restore.
In Revelation 2, Jesus spoke to the church in Ephesus.
He acknowledged their works, labor, perseverance, and discernment.
This was not a congregation doing absolutely nothing.
They were active.
They endured.
They rejected false teaching.
Yet Jesus said:
“Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.” (Revelation 2:4, KJV)
Then He commanded them to remember, repent, and return to the works they did at first.
Notice the mercy hidden inside that confrontation.
Jesus didn't merely expose what had gone wrong.
He called them back.
He did not treat spiritual decline as something to celebrate or excuse.
But neither did He present repentance as a meaningless act.
He called His people to return.
And perhaps that's exactly what you need to hear.
You don't need another month of pretending.
You don't need to manufacture an impressive spiritual image.
You don't need to compare your prayer life to someone else's.
You need to come honestly before Christ.
“Lord, I have allowed other things to occupy the place that belongs to You.”
“Lord, I have become distracted.”
“Lord, I've been seeking Your gifts while neglecting Your presence.”
“Lord, I have called You my Savior while resisting Your authority in parts of my life.”
And then something extraordinary happens when we understand the Gospel.
We realize that Jesus is not calling us to earn His love by becoming better at time management.
He's calling us to repentance and faith because He is the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
This is where Christianity differs from a motivational speech about productivity.
A motivational speaker might tell you to wake up earlier, eliminate distractions, and master your morning routine.
Some of that advice might be useful.
But it cannot reconcile a sinner to a holy God.
A perfectly organized schedule cannot wash away sin.
A thousand consecutive mornings of Bible reading cannot purchase forgiveness.
A spotless attendance record cannot make someone righteous before God.
Only Jesus Christ can save.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
And verse 10 reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
Grace comes first.
Good works follow.
We do not seek God to purchase salvation.
We seek Him because, through Christ, we have been invited into a restored relationship with the Father.
We do not obey to force Jesus to love us.
We learn to obey because He has loved us with a love demonstrated at the cross.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we fixed our schedules.
Not after we became disciplined enough.
Not after we finally looked respectable.
Christ died for sinners.
Think about that for a moment.
The One who deserves every moment of your life willingly entered human history to rescue people who had spent their lives turning away from Him.
He knew betrayal.
He knew rejection.
He knew suffering.
He carried our sins to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That is the heart of the Gospel proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The resurrection means that our hope is not built on the memory of a dead religious teacher.
Our hope rests in the living Lord Jesus Christ.
And the same Savior who calls us to repent is the Savior through whom forgiveness and new life are offered.
This is why your story does not have to end with spiritual neglect.
This is why the believer who has drifted can repent and return.
This is why the person who has been hiding behind religious appearances can finally tell the truth.
This is why the exhausted Christian can stop confusing constant activity with faithful devotion.
And this is why someone who has never truly surrendered to Christ can turn to Him today.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that disciplined people can save themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners and transforms those who belong to Him.
From scandal to grace… because Jesus rewrites everything.
But grace does not mean our priorities are irrelevant.
The grace that forgives us also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
Jesus said in Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (KJV)
That word daily matters.
Following Jesus is not merely a decision remembered from years ago.
It is a life of continuing dependence, repentance, and obedience.
Not sinless perfection.
Not an uninterrupted record of spiritual success.
But a real relationship with a real Savior who increasingly changes the direction of our lives.
And that brings us back to your schedule.
What if you stopped looking at it merely as a calendar of obligations and began looking at it as a window into what you value?
What if you examined your last seven days without making excuses or immediately condemning yourself?
Where did your attention go?
What captured your imagination?
What did you sacrifice for?
What did you consistently postpone?
Did you make room for God's Word?
Did you speak to Him in prayer?
Did you show patience to your family?
Did you practice integrity when nobody was watching?
Did you love someone who could give you nothing in return?
Did you turn away from temptation?
Did you seek forgiveness when you were wrong?
Did you use your resources with gratitude and generosity?
Did your ordinary decisions reflect the teachings of Christ?
And when you failed, did you return to Him in repentance, or did you simply grow comfortable with the distance?
These questions aren't intended to create a competition over who spends the most hours in religious activity.
They are invitations to examine the direction of our hearts.
Because a father working long hours with honesty, praying as he travels, and lovingly caring for his children may be honoring Christ through his ordinary responsibilities.
A mother holding a sick child at three in the morning may be demonstrating sacrificial love without having a quiet hour to herself.
A student studying diligently while refusing to cheat may be honoring God in the classroom.
A nurse caring compassionately for patients may be serving Christ through faithful work.
Colossians 3:23 says:
“And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.” (KJV)
Whatever you do.
Not only what you do inside a church building.
Not only what you do with an open Bible.
Your ordinary life can become an arena of worship.
But here's the distinction.
There is a difference between inviting Jesus into your responsibilities and using your responsibilities as a permanent excuse to avoid Him.
Only you and God fully know what is happening in your heart.
And perhaps that's why this message feels uncomfortable.
Because deep down, you know there are things you could surrender.
Maybe it's the endless scrolling.
Maybe it's the entertainment that keeps pulling you toward temptation.
Maybe it's the bitterness you keep rehearsing.
Maybe it's the obsession with success that has turned your career into your identity.
Maybe it's the relationship you refuse to examine in the light of Scripture.
Maybe it's the fear of disappointing people that has become stronger than your desire to obey God.
Maybe it's simply the habit of giving Jesus whatever attention remains after everyone and everything else has taken their share.
And perhaps the hardest realization is this:
You've been asking God to bless a life in which you rarely consult Him.
Not because He is absent.
But because you've become accustomed to moving ahead without seeking His wisdom.
Yet even now, the invitation of Jesus remains astonishingly tender.
In Matthew 11:28, He says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
He does not say, “Come to Me once you've mastered your schedule.”
He does not say, “Come to Me once you've proven you deserve another chance.”
He says, “Come unto me.”
That invitation is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to come under the care and lordship of the One who can change us.
So maybe tonight, instead of promising God a dramatic spiritual transformation you haven't thought through, begin with an honest prayer.
Put the phone down.
Open the Scriptures.
Read a passage carefully.
Speak to God about what is actually happening inside you.
Not the polished version.
Not the version you present at church.
The real version.
Tell Him where you are distracted.
Tell Him what you are afraid to surrender.
Confess the sin you have been excusing.
Ask for wisdom concerning your responsibilities.
Ask Him to teach you to love what He loves.
And tomorrow, begin practicing what you have prayed.
Maybe you set aside a realistic period to read and meditate on Scripture.
Maybe you pray during your commute.
Maybe you turn off an app that has been consuming your attention.
Maybe you apologize to someone you have hurt.
Maybe you finally reconnect with a faithful Christian community.
Maybe you choose generosity over another unnecessary purchase.
Maybe you begin discipling your children through ordinary conversations.
Maybe you stop treating Sunday worship as optional whenever something more entertaining appears.
None of these actions earns your place in God's family.
But they can become meaningful expressions of a heart learning to seek Him first.
And don't underestimate small beginnings.
A faithful Christian life is not usually built through one spectacular emotional moment.
It is formed through continuing trust in Christ, obedience to His Word, repentance when we fail, and the gracious work of the Holy Spirit.
Some days will feel beautiful.
Other days will feel ordinary.
There will be mornings when Scripture seems to speak directly into your situation.
There will also be mornings when you're tired and distracted.
There will be seasons of joy.
And seasons when your prayers are mixed with tears.
Faithfulness does not mean every moment feels spiritually extraordinary.
It means continuing to turn toward the Lord, even when obedience is difficult.
And please remember this:
Jesus is not another task you must squeeze into an already exhausting life.
He is Lord over the life you already have.
He is not asking you to abandon the people you are responsible for loving.
He is teaching you how to love them under His authority.
He is not necessarily calling you to leave your profession.
He is calling you to follow Him within it.
He is not asking you to neglect rest.
He is the One who invites the weary to come to Him.
He is not calling you to become obsessed with measuring every minute.
He is calling you to trust, love, and obey Him.
Because the goal is not to build a schedule that makes you look holy.
The goal is to become a person whose life increasingly reflects the holiness, mercy, truth, and love of Jesus Christ.
And if this message has uncovered something you've been hiding, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply agreeing with it.
Be honest.
Not for appearances.
Not to impress strangers.
But because sometimes acknowledging the truth is the beginning of a needed conversation.
Or, if you're struggling and don't know where to begin, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You don't need to share private details you aren't comfortable revealing.

And if you've experienced God's grace in a season of spiritual dryness, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading these words may desperately need to know that repentance and restoration are possible through Christ.
There may be another person in your life who needs this message too.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to publicly accuse.
Someone you love.
A brother who has become spiritually exhausted.
A sister who feels far from God.
A friend who has been overwhelmed by work.
A parent carrying burdens nobody sees.
A believer who still attends church but quietly feels disconnected from Jesus.
Or someone who has never understood why the Gospel is about more than religious routines.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because the truth of Scripture may encourage someone who would never openly admit they're struggling.
Not because every word in it is equally important, but because the Scriptures it points to deserve more than a passing glance.
Come back to Matthew 6:33.
Come back to Luke 10:38–42.
Come back to Revelation 2:1–7.
Come back to Ephesians 2:8–10.
And above all, come back to Jesus.
Our desire is to keep pointing people beyond temporary inspiration and toward lasting discipleship rooted in God's Word.
And there's something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior exists because we believe the message of Jesus Christ is too important to be treated as just another passing social media post.

Behind every article, every devotional, every biblical resource, and every effort to reach another person is a continuing commitment to share the Gospel, encourage repentance, strengthen believers, and make discipleship resources more accessible.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Christian faith, develop spiritual maturity, and continue following Jesus beyond a single article.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support can be part of their Christian generosity and stewardship.
But an important biblical distinction matters here.
Christians differ in how they understand the application of tithing under the New Covenant. But Scripture is clear that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
The Greek word ἱλαρόν (hilaron) describes a cheerful or glad giver.
The point is that genuine generosity should come from a willing heart.
You do not have to pay to be part of the family of God.
Those things cannot be bought.
It can be a voluntary offering of support, given in gratitude to God and in service to a mission you believe is worthwhile.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Your financial situation does not determine your value before God.
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
But with gratitude, wisdom, and a willing heart.
Your life is moving.
Your days are passing.
Your habits are forming you.
Your choices are shaping what you love.
Psalm 90:12 says:
“So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the opening words are:
לִמְנוֹת יָמֵינוּ כֵּן הוֹדַע
Limnot yameinu ken hoda.
The prayer asks God to teach us to number our days.
It is not merely about calculating how long we might live.
It is about recognizing life's brevity and learning to live wisely before God.
One day, the messages demanding your attention will stop.
The deadlines will end.
The social media trends will be forgotten.
The things that once seemed urgent may no longer matter.
And you will have lived the days entrusted to you.
That reality is not meant to drive you into panic.
It is meant to awaken wisdom.
Because you cannot go back and relive yesterday.
But by God's grace, you can respond faithfully today.
You can repent today.
You can seek reconciliation today.
You can open His Word today.
You can pray today.
You can love the people entrusted to your care today.
You can stop postponing obedience today.
And if you've never truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ, you can turn to Him today.
Don't wait until your life looks religious enough.
Come to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Trust Him.
Turn from sin.
Receive His Word.
Follow Him.
And if you already belong to Christ but have drifted, don't mistake His call to repentance for a declaration that restoration is impossible.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
What a beautiful promise.
Not permission to hide.
Not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
But assurance that forgiveness and cleansing are found in God's faithfulness through Jesus Christ.
Maybe your schedule has revealed a painful truth.
Maybe you've been busy with everything except the things that matter most.
Maybe you've become distracted, spiritually cold, or divided in your loyalties.
Then let this be the moment you stop pretending.
Not the moment you surrender to despair.
The moment you surrender to Jesus.
You don't need to rewrite the past to begin walking faithfully today.
You need the grace of the One who redeems sinners and transforms lives.
So when tomorrow morning comes, and your phone begins demanding your attention again, remember this question:
Who truly has first place in my heart?
And don't answer too quickly.
Bring the question before God.
Let Scripture search you.
Let the Holy Spirit convict you.
Let the Gospel comfort you.
And let the lordship of Jesus reshape the ordinary moments of your life.
Because the greatest tragedy would not simply be discovering that you had a busy schedule.
It would be spending your life declaring that Jesus was your greatest treasure while continually giving your heart to lesser things.
And the beautiful hope of the Gospel is that your story does not have to remain that way.
Don't spend your whole life making room for everything else, only to discover that you kept postponing the One who gave His life to bring you home.
